central_topic: Sensitivity of ridge-regularized Bradley-Terry rankings to small, influence-selected row deletions, comparing crowdsourced Chatbot Arena preferences with historical NBA game outcomes using exact refits and random/high-loss deletion controls.
core_methods: Centered Bradley-Terry estimation with half-win ties and fixed mean-loss ridge regularization
Clean-Hessian inverse influence for leader-contender contrasts and frozen nested deletion prefixes
Bounded contender screening followed by converged retained-data refits using aggregated pair sufficient statistics
Retained-Hessian one-step Newton proxy for bounded shortlist expansion; no observed aggregate improvement over the exact-refit selector
Normalized pairwise ranking inversions and original-leader rank displacement; conditional group-bootstrap refits of fixed deletion masks
comparators: Uniform random row deletion and clean-fit high-log-loss disagreement deletion, with unchanged-data and row-permutation controls
First-order influence and finite-sample data-removal robustness versus exact retained-data refitting
Preference-vote manipulation as related threat-model context, not an implemented vote-insertion baseline
benchmarks: Chatbot Arena arena-human-preference-55k pinned snapshot, partition-specific largest connected component
FiveThirtyEight nba-elo/nbaallelo.csv pinned historical game snapshot, deduplicated with _iscopy=0 and restricted to the partition-specific largest connected component
result_driven_themes: Bounded exact-refit contender selection improved the recorded search aggregate over clean-Hessian-only selection; retained-curvature expansion tied that aggregate rather than improving it
Final aggregate inversion disruption exceeded random and disagreement deletion, but disagreement-relative gains differ by dataset and deletion budget
Final conditional group-bootstrap gains relative to disagreement deletion are negative on average for Arena and positive on average for NBA; these are fixed-mask refits, not reoptimized attacks
Identical candidate scores across five final seeds and row-permutation controls do not establish independent dataset replication or causal effects of evaluation design

queries.query: "Rank Analysis of Incomplete Block Designs: I. The Method of Paired Comparisons"
queries.rationale: The actual estimator is Bradley-Terry on both Arena and NBA. Resolve only the supplied Bradley and Terry (1952) work, DOI 10.2307/2334029; distinguish its foundation from this run-specific mean-loss ridge and tie conventions.

Clean-Hessian inverse-gradient contrasts determine every legal deletion prefix. Resolve only the supplied Koh and Liang (2017) work, arXiv:1703.04730, for influence-function context; it does not establish accuracy of this run-specific shortlist or finite deletions.

queries.query: "An Automatic Finite-Sample Robustness Metric: When Can Dropping a Little Data Make a Big Difference?"
queries.rationale: Small-fraction deletion robustness and the gap between local approximations and retained-data conclusions are central to the exact-refit selector and heterogeneous baseline gains. Resolve only the supplied Broderick, Giordano and Meager (2020) work, arXiv:2011.14999; do not claim globally minimal deletion sets or universal fragility.

queries.query: "Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference"
queries.rationale: Arena crowdsourced preferences are actually evaluated, unlike the proposed MT-Bench human/GPT-4 comparison. Resolve only the supplied Chiang et al. (2024) work, arXiv:2403.04132; separately retain the pinned 55k dataset provenance rather than treating the platform paper as snapshot documentation.

NBA is the actual second evaluation design. Restrict resolution to the supplied fivethirtyeight/data repository at commit 4c1ff5e3aef1816ae04af63218015066e186c147, its nba-elo documentation and original dataset. Cite data provenance, not a guessed paper; Elo labels identify the source, whereas this run fits Bradley-Terry to game outcomes.

queries.query: "Improving Your Model Ranking on Chatbot Arena by Vote Rigging"
queries.rationale: Resolve only the explicitly supplied Min et al. (2025) work, arXiv:2501.17858, to distinguish deliberate preference manipulation from this run’s constrained row deletions. Random and high-loss deletion are the measured controls; vote insertion, flipping and this publication’s algorithms were not evaluated here.
